body: For bitcoin, the June closing low near $58,500 is now the key level. A clean break would put the next on-chain support clusters, around $57,000 and then $47,000, in play, and would probably trigger more selling from miners whose costs sit well above the price. For Strategy shareholders, forced selling by index funds around the November 30 MSCI removal could widen the discount further before any rebound. Heavy options positioning could make moves in either direction more violent. A recovery in the ratio back above 1, as happened in July, would be the clearest sign that sellers are finished. JPMorgan reads Strategy's record discount to its bitcoin holdings as a sign that selling may be nearly exhausted, but ETF outflows, struggling miners and a looming index removal mean the market has yet to confirm a bottom. Strategy, the world's largest corporate holder of bitcoin, has fallen to a record discount to the value of its bitcoin holdings on JPMorgan's preferred measure. The bank's analysts see this as a possible sign that selling in the cryptocurrency is close to capitulation. Several other indicators suggest the bottom may not be in yet. According to BeInCrypto , which reported the findings, the bank's Flows and Liquidity team calculates that the company formerly known as MicroStrategy was valued at 0.88 times its bitcoin holdings on Wednesday. The measure compares the bitcoin holdings with the company's enterprise value, which includes its debt and preferred stock as well as its equity. The previous low of 0.89 came in late June, when bitcoin posted a closing low of around $58,500. The ratio then recovered above 1 by early July. Strategy's own dashboard, which uses a different calculation, shows a reading of around 0.94. Readings this deep tend to reflect extreme pessimism, and similar conditions have often appeared near market lows. There is a complication this time. Strategy is due to be removed from MSCI indexes on November 30, which will force index-tracking funds to sell the shares regardless of value. That could push the discount wider for technical rather than fundamental reasons. Speculative positioning is also unusually heavy. Executive chairman Michael Saylor says outstanding options on the stock equal about 61% of its market value, compared with around 14% for Tesla. The flow picture remains difficult. JPMorgan notes that investors kept pulling money from BlackRock's spot bitcoin ETF even during a brief price rebound, and at a faster pace than in the May to June sell-off. Miners are under strain too. The bank puts the cost of producing one bitcoin at about $86,000, up from $85,000 in September, well above the current price near $60,500. Estimates based on MARA Holdings' filings put costs closer to $63,000, a level the price is now testing. Higher-cost producers may have to sell reserves to stay afloat. Others are more cautious. One crypto research firm says only two of its 13 historical bottom signals had triggered as of November 22, and that after seven similar support breakdowns, the eventual low came at least 17% further down. The head of research at an on-chain analytics firm warned that bottoming and recovery have historically taken months, even with short-term rallies along the way. On-chain cost-basis data points to resistance near $63,000, with around $57,000 seen as the critical threshold below the June low. Deeper support clusters sit near $47,000 and $38,000. For now, the June low near $58,500 is the line to watch. A record discount at Strategy suggests sellers may be close to exhausted, but the market has not yet confirmed a bottom. title: Kiwi edges higher as official NZ election count confirms a hung parliament
summary: The muted reaction suggests NZD traders are pricing politics as noise unless talks break down. The tail risk is a failed negotiation and a fresh election, which would bring a longer period of uncertainty and could weigh on the currency and New Zealand government bonds. Coalition deals that come with large fiscal commitments are the other thing to watch, especially for bond yields. Outside Wellington, the kiwi remains tied to global risk sentiment and the US dollar. With the Fed widely expected to hike in December and AI-related volatility still unsettling equities, those forces are likely to outweigh the election result. --- Earlier: NZ consumer confidence breaks 100 as falling fuel prices cool inflation fears --- New Zealand's official count has confirmed a hung parliament, but the kiwi's small rise suggests currency traders see coalition talks as a political puzzle rather than an economic threat, at least for now. Summary: The New Zealand dollar edged higher after official election results confirmed a hung parliament The incumbent centre-right coalition will need the centrist Opportunity Party to govern The small move suggests markets see limited immediate economic risk from coalition talks A prolonged stalemate or a fresh election remains the main political risk for the currency Global risk appetite, the US dollar and the RBNZ outlook are likely to remain the bigger drivers The New Zealand dollar edged higher on Friday after official election results confirmed a hung parli
body: The muted reaction suggests NZD traders are pricing politics as noise unless talks break down. The tail risk is a failed negotiation and a fresh election, which would bring a longer period of uncertainty and could weigh on the currency and New Zealand government bonds. Coalition deals that come with large fiscal commitments are the other thing to watch, especially for bond yields. Outside Wellington, the kiwi remains tied to global risk sentiment and the US dollar. With the Fed widely expected to hike in December and AI-related volatility still unsettling equities, those forces are likely to outweigh the election result. New Zealand's official count has confirmed a hung parliament, but the kiwi's small rise suggests currency traders see coalition talks as a political puzzle rather than an economic threat, at least for now. The New Zealand dollar edged higher on Friday after official election results confirmed a hung parliament. The modest move suggests currency traders see little immediate economic risk in the drawn-out coalition talks that now lie ahead. The final count from the Electoral Commission left the incumbent centre-right coalition short of a majority on its own, so it will need the support of the centrist Opportunity Party to govern. The result removes some of the uncertainty that hung over the preliminary election-night tally, even if it doesn't yet settle who will form the next government. The kiwi's gain of a few points was small by any measure, and the lack of a sharper reaction is telling. Political uncertainty in New Zealand rarely moves the currency for long, and markets appear to be treating the result as a question of coalition arithmetic rather than a shift in economic direction. Having a centrist kingmaker, rather than a party on either ideological flank, may also limit concern about abrupt changes to fiscal policy. The risks haven't disappeared. Negotiations could stretch on for weeks, and if no workable government emerges, New Zealand could face a fresh election. A prolonged stalemate, or a deal that came with significant spending or tax commitments, could test the currency and the local bond market. For now, though, traders seem content to wait. In the meantime, the kiwi's direction is likely to depend on more familiar drivers. Global risk appetite has been fragile amid turmoil in AI-linked stocks, and the New Zealand dollar, like its Australian counterpart, tends to struggle when investors retreat from risk. The US dollar has been supported by expectations of a Federal Reserve rate hike in December. Moves in those markets, along with the outlook for the Reserve Bank of New Zealand, are likely to matter more for the kiwi in the coming days than developments in Wellington. Traders will watch for any signs of progress in coalition talks, but unless the politics turn messy, the election looks set to remain a sideshow for the currency. title: NZ consumer confidence breaks 100 as falling fuel prices cool inflation fears
summary: Households' inflation expectations have fallen sharply from their April peak, which eases one worry for the Reserve Bank of New Zealand. That leans slightly against any hawkish shift in the policy outlook and is a mild negative for the New Zealand dollar at the margin. The survey's market impact is usually small, though, and moves in global risk appetite and the US dollar are likely to matter more for the currency. The main sensitivity to watch is oil: these readings now follow pump prices closely, so a renewed jump in crude would probably undo much of this month's improvement. --- Cheaper fuel has pushed Kiwi consumer confidence back above 100 and pulled inflation expectations to a 22-month low, but households still feel better about the future than the present and remain wary of big purchases. Summary: Consumer confidence rose 4 points to 100.2 in November, the highest since January but still below the long-run average of 112 The future conditions index rose to around 111 and the current conditions index to around 84 Two-year inflation expectations fell to 3.9% from 4.2%, the lowest since January 2025 and well down from April's 6.6% The 12-month economic outlook improved to a net 6% pessimistic, while the five-year outlook rose to a net 16% optimistic A net 12% still see it as a bad time to buy major household items, a 6-point improvement House price expectations rose to 2.3% from 2.0%, still below the 3.5% average New Zealand consumer confidence climbed back above the 100
body: Households' inflation expectations have fallen sharply from their April peak, which eases one worry for the Reserve Bank of New Zealand. That leans slightly against any hawkish shift in the policy outlook and is a mild negative for the New Zealand dollar at the margin. The survey's market impact is usually small, though, and moves in global risk appetite and the US dollar are likely to matter more for the currency. The main sensitivity to watch is oil: these readings now follow pump prices closely, so a renewed jump in crude would probably undo much of this month's improvement. Cheaper fuel has pushed Kiwi consumer confidence back above 100 and pulled inflation expectations to a 22-month low, but households still feel better about the future than the present and remain wary of big purchases. New Zealand consumer confidence climbed back above the 100 mark in November. Falling fuel prices pulled households' inflation expectations to their lowest level in nearly two years, and both the current and future measures of sentiment improved. The ANZ-Roy Morgan Consumer Confidence index rose 4 points to 100.2, its strongest reading since January, according to the survey released on Friday. That is still well short of the long-run average of 112, so the recovery from April's low near 80 is not complete. Both components improved. The future conditions index rose to around 111 from 106, while the current conditions index edged up to around 84 from 81. The biggest shift came in inflation expectations. Households now see prices rising 3.9% a year over the next two years, down from 4.2% in October and the lowest since January 2025. That is a steep fall from April's 6.6%, when a spike in pump prices pushed expectations sharply higher. The survey's authors noted that consumers' price expectations fell slightly more than fuel prices over the month, after tracking them almost one-for-one earlier in the year. They also pointed out that inflation expectations and confidence have moved in opposite directions in recent years, which suggests the two are linked. The economic outlook improved but stayed gloomy for the next 12 months. A net 6% of respondents expect bad times for the economy over that period, compared with a net 13% a month earlier. The five-year view rose to a net 16% positive from 8%, close to its long-run average of 19%. Views on household finances were mixed. A net 20% said they were worse off than a year ago, a marginal improvement. A net 22% expect to be better off a year from now, down from 24% but far above April's low of 3%. Appetite for spending remains soft. A net 12% still think it is a bad time to buy a major household item, although that is a 6-point improvement on October. House price expectations rose to 2.3% from 2.0%, still well below the survey's 3.5% average. The survey's authors described the overall mood as below par, citing broader cost-of-living pressures and a soft labour market. They cautioned that consumers' inflation expectations carry less weight for monetary policy than those of businesses, which actually set prices. Households feel better about the future than about the present, which suggests they are not yet ready to spend freely. The next survey is due on December 18. Your market education doesn't end here. body: Tanker Traffic at Hormuz Ticks Up Despite Intensified Attacks Alex Kimani is a veteran finance writer, investor, engineer and researcher for Safehaven.com. Oil prices continued to recover from their recent slump, with renewed Middle East supply threats outweighing earlier global surplus concerns. Brent crude for January delivery climbed 1.3% to trade at $95.90 per barrel at 12.00 pm ET on Thursday, a sharp rise after closing at $89.37/bbl on Monday while the corresponding WTI crude contract was up 1.2% to change hands at $84.65/ bbl. Yemen's Houthi forces claimed on Wednesday that their strikes on Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura oil refinery and export complex caused fires, with satellite imagery from NASA and Planet Labs revealing thick black smoke over the site. The Houthis also claimed multiple strikes on Riyadh's financial district, where Saudi civil defense reported 11 people were injured on Tuesday after a strike hit a tower housing the Public Investment Fund for the second time in under a week. U.S. commercial crude oil inventories rose by 1.1 million barrels to 418.9 million barrels in the week ended November 20, marking a third consecutive weekly build as higher net imports and domestic output outweighed increased refinery runs while crude exports dropped to their lowest level since early August amid higher freight costs and softer Asian demand. Traders will be watching the November 29 OPEC+ ministerial meeting, where members are set to discuss 2027 production policy amid competing views on potential supply surpluses and internal quota disputes. And now, oil and commodity experts at Standard Chartered have weighed in, saying that oil prices are unlikely to sink below recent lows, with further downside needing clearer evidence of sustained inventory builds or a faster recovery in physical supply, even as the geopolitical uncertainty continues to complicate the outlook. Brent crude spent much of the past week consolidating around the low $90s/bbl, following a sharp correction from the late-October highs, before slipping below $90/bbl on Monday with the $89.37/bbl settlement the lowest in nearly three months. Related: Goldman Sachs Sees U.S. Natural Gas Demand Surging on Data Center Boom According to the analysts, the price action reflects the increasingly entrenched bearish fundamental narrative, which was reinforced by the IEA’s substantial upward revision to Q4 supply. The IEA raised its Q4 supply estimate by 3.3mb/d in its November Oil Market Report, reflecting a faster recovery in Gulf production and exports than previously expected. This has reinforced expectations of a return to surplus by the end of the year, coupled with a more substantial build in 2027. However, StanChart says that the recent price correction has already discounted much of the anticipated supply surplus, implying that a sustained move lower may require evidence that the surplus will emerge sooner, be larger, or persist for longer than currently expected, rather than simply confirming existing forecasts. That said, there’s an ongoing broad decline across refined product prices, refining margins and freight rates, suggesting that some of the exceptional tightness associated with geopolitical disruptions is beginning to unwind. According to StanChart, European jet fuel (NWE Jet CIF cargo balance of month) and Asian fuel oil (Singapore 380 M1) prices declined 24% and 31% MTD, respectively, while the European diesel crack (ICE gasoil/Brent spread) has fallen 21%, indicating that the adjustment extends beyond falling crude prices. Refining economics have also weakened, with both Asian FCC margins and NWE hydrocracking margins down 25% MTD. Meanwhile, Middle East-to-China (TD3C) clean product freight rates have declined 27%, while dirty VLCC freight rates on the Gulf-to-China route have fallen 55% MTD. body: Tanker Traffic at Hormuz Ticks Up Despite Intensified Attacks Tom majored in International Business at Amsterdam’s Higher School of Economics and later completed an Executive MBA in Energy Transition at the University of Groningen.… Ukraine's sinking of a Russian warship in Benghazi on November 22 is the spark that could ignite another civil war in Libya, just as Tripoli is pitching foreign oil companies at an energy summit for the $20 billion it says it needs to lift output to 2 million barrels a day. Two officers of eastern strongman Khalifa Haftar's Libyan National Army (LNA) died of their wounds on November 24, and the LNA has vowed to retaliate "at the appropriate time and place." Haftar flew to Turkey the same day on his first known visit , and on November 25 his parliament published the Turkey-Libya maritime deal in Libya's official gazette, completing a ratification that opens waters off the eastern coast to Turkish exploration. On the day of Haftar's visit, EU Mediterranean Commissioner Dubravka Šuica told the European Parliament that the deal "is null and void." Everyone is scrambling for leverage, and there's plenty of it flying around, making this difficult to contain. Ukrainian sea drones hit the Russian corvette Merkury in the civilian part of Benghazi's port , next to a naval base, where it had docked to refuel and resupply under a cooperation agreement between Russia and Haftar's eastern government. Moscow has no port of its own in the southern Mediterranean, and it has funded projects at Haftar-controlled air bases including al-Jufra and al-Khadim. The drones were most likely launched from Misrata, a western city where Abdulhamid Dbeibah's Tripoli government hosts Ukrainian drone teams and Turkish troops. Moscow has a reason to strike western Libya, and any strike launched from Haftar's bases would make his family a party to it. Related: Tanker Traffic at Hormuz Ticks Up Despite Intensified Attacks The strike puts at risk a business partnership between the two families' heirs, documented by the UN. Ibrahim Dbeibah, the prime minister's nephew and adviser, and Saddam Haftar, Khalifa Haftar's son and deputy, had built control over the National Oil Corporation (NOC) "at every level of the decision-making process," according to the UN Panel of Experts' final report . Their deal created the Arkenu Oil Company, which diverted more than $3 billion between January 2024 and November 2025 alone through illicit fuel exports from Benghazi, Ras Lanuf and Tobruk, all ports outside the NOC's control. The UN also documented an arms procurement pact between Dbeibah's government and Haftar's forces under their joint patronage. It covered vehicles shipped to Misrata and Benghazi under an end-user certificate the prime minister signed in his capacity as defense minister. By the UN panel's count, Libya's oil revenue in 2025, excluding royalties and taxes, came to $18.78 billion, against the roughly $27 billion it should have earned. Saddam Haftar's office and a Tripoli government official deny that either has any connection to Arkenu. The rival legislatures have agreed on a unified budget, and Belqasim Haftar runs the state fund rebuilding Derna. Washington is drafting a merger that would keep Abdulhamid Dbeibah as prime minister and seat Saddam Haftar at the head of the Presidential Council. Armed factions in the west are resisting the plan, and Washington has warned it could take measures against anyone who blocks it, Al-Monitor reported . Earlier this month, an influential Misrata military body demanded an immediate end to the Arkenu deal, declaring that "Libyan oil is a red line." On November 24, two days after the Ukrainian strike, Dbeibah's government asked a Tripoli court to annul the contract . body: Tanker Traffic at Hormuz Ticks Up Despite Intensified Attacks Haley Zaremba is an energy journalist and researcher with more than a decade of professional experience covering global energy systems, land and natural resources, and… The artificial intelligence boom is putting unprecedented pressure on global energy grids. The energy needs of planned data centers outstrip planned energy additions in many places where hyperscalers are developing massive campuses. As a result, the private and public sector alike are increasingly and urgently adopting an all-of-the-above approach to energy development, increasing the scale and lifespan of fossil fuels and renewable energies alike, while also pouring funding into the research and development of next-gen energy alternatives. One of those promising energy alternatives is enhanced geothermal. Geothermal energy itself is nothing new – about 85 percent of all houses in Iceland have been heated with geothermal energy for years now. But that kind of geothermal energy is only viable in geologically anomalous places like Iceland, where the heat from the Earth’s core naturally breaks through to the surface in the form of hot springs, geysers, or other forms of heat vents. But the emerging field of enhanced geothermal seeks to make geothermal energy viable anywhere on Earth by digging deep enough to access that heat and pump it to the surface. In order to do that, geothermal startups and research projects are borrowing technology from a sector that knows a whole lot about drilling – Big Oil. That’s right, the next big thing in clean and green energy may come in the form of none other than fracking. Hydraulic fracturing could allow geothermal initiatives to cost-effectively drill to extreme depths where thermal heat is naturally abundant in order to provide a source of zero-emissions energy 24 hours a day, seven days a week. “If you drill down deep enough — three, four, even six kilometers — you reach the point where the crust is uniformly hot,” University of California Irvine engineer Mohammad Javad Abdolhosseini Qomi was quoted in a recent article from the UC Newsroom. “Then you can drill horizontally, create fractures, and pipe in water.” The rock heats the water, turning it to steam that can run turbines that generate electricity. However, we still have a long way to go before that can be achieved at a commercially viable scale. “There is more than enough potential geothermal energy underground to power the entire United States, but unlocking it safely and economically is still a major challenge,” Qomi went on to say. Scientists at the University of California are one of many groups trying to find a pathway toward bringing enhanced geothermal out of lab-based modeling and into the market. Some private companies are likewise working on employing hydraulic fracturing technology to unlock commercial enhanced geothermal. Meanwhile, others are employing techniques from the field of nuclear fusion, using a vacuum-tube gyrotron to vaporize rock molecules with high-frequency electromagnetic waves down a borehole. The round-the-clock energy potential of enhanced geothermal is just one of the sector’s benefits. Another critical advantage of the sector is its broad, bipartisan appeal as one of the vanishingly few forms of clean energy to receive equally enthusiastic policy support under the Biden and Trump administrations. The UC project is backed by the U.S. Department of Energy’s Genesis Mission as part of this push. The Department of Energy is bullish about the potential of geothermal in the future of the United States’ energy mix. Projections from the agency state that enhanced geothermal projects could provide about 90 gigawatts of carbon-free energy in the U.S. by 2050 , or approximately enough to power at least 65 million homes. title: BC Securities Commission stays insider trading charges in case linked to former gold junior CFO
summary: Investment fund operator had been charged with two counts of alleged insider trading.
body: Investment fund operator had been charged with two counts of alleged insider trading. The BC Securities Commission said Wednesday that the BC Prosecution Service have stayed charges in an alleged insider trading scheme. Douwe van Hees had been charged in 2025 on two counts of prohibited insider trading under the Criminal Code after an investigation by the BCSC. The investment fund operator had been charged for one count using inside information obtained from Shaun Pollard, who was Chief Financial Officer at Westhaven Gold at the time of the alleged offences and possessed that information by virtue of their employment. Pollard co-founded Westhaven Gold in 2010 and served as its CFO for over 14 years, until February 2025. All charges against Pollard were dropped in October 2025. A second charge was brought against van Hees for using inside information possessed by virtue of van Hees being a shareholder and/or having a business or professional relationship with an issuer. In a May bail hearing in Vancouver Provincial Court, van Hees was granted release on a number of conditions, including that he pay a C$150,000 deposit into court, the BCSC said. Van Hees’ lawyer, Joseph Saulnier of Martland Saulnier, told Business in Vancouver he asked the Commission for a clear statement, but it was not provided. Saulnier also told the newspaper van Hees adamantly maintained his innocence.

body: Bitcoin’s next big move is up for debate. A Polymarket contract with nearly $96.2 million in volume tracks how far BTC could fall or climb before the end of 2026. title: Brent settles higher as mine strikes, refinery attack stoke Middle East supply concerns - Yahoo Finance
body: CALGARY, Nov 26 (Reuters) - Crude oil prices rose on Thursday after Yemen's Houthis said they hit Saudi Arabia's largest oil refinery, and Iran said mines struck ships in the Strait of Hormuz, ‌reviving concerns about supply disruptions. Brent crude futures settled at $96.57 a barrel, up $1.96, or 1.2%. US West Texas ‌Intermediate crude futures, which did not settle on Thursday because of the US Thanksgiving holiday, were up $1.16, or 1.39%, at $84.84 as of 1:21 ​p.m. ET (1821 GMT). A series of events this week increased geopolitical worries and the Middle East risk premium. On Wednesday, the Iran-aligned Houthis said they had attacked Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura oil refinery, part of a complex that also serves as a major export terminal for Saudi crude. At the same time, shipping has been disrupted through the Strait of Hormuz, where oil ‌supply had been recovering to levels close ⁠to those before the Iran war. On Thursday, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said two tankers had exploded and caught fire after hitting sea mines north of Oman's Khasab port while attempting ⁠to cross the strait. One of the vessels was a supertanker carrying more than 2 million barrels of crude oil, the Guards said. "This is keeping the market on edge into the (Thanksgiving) holiday," said Phil Flynn, senior analyst at Price Futures Group. While data will ​probably ​show a small global supply surplus in October, said Commodity ​Context founder Rory Johnston, the outlook for crude ‌prices is bullish. He cited slowing Hormuz flows, low inventories, and what he called "known, acute risk" to approximately 15% of global supplies. "My view is that we were oversold when (Brent) was dipping below $90," Johnston said. "It was only a matter of time before we tightened again." OPEC+ ministers will hold meetings on Sunday to decide their 2027 output policy. They face the challenge of balancing output with the United Arab Emirates no longer in the group, and ‌with Iraq and Kazakhstan pressing OPEC+ to raise its estimate ​of their oil production capacity. Two people with knowledge of the matter said OPEC+ ​may roll over its current oil output targets ​at the meeting for at least the first quarter of 2027. US crude stocks rose by ‌1.1 million barrels to 418.9 million barrels in ​the week ended November 20, ​the Energy Information Administration said. That supported prices because analysts had expected a rise of 1.5 million barrels. [EIA/S] In Asia, Thailand's Bangchak Corp said it had shut all production units at its Phra Khanong oil refinery in ​Bangkok after a fire. A drone attack ‌at the Slavyansk ECO oil refinery in Russia's southern Krasnodar region also led to a fire, ​inflicting serious damage. (Reporting by Amanda Stephenson in Calgary, Seher Dareen in London and Sudarshan Varadhan in ​Singapore; Editing by Bill Berkrot, Rod Nickel and Chris Reese)

body: There are plenty of theories about why the stock market is crashing. Some blame overvalued AI stocks or the ongoing Iran war. Others point to the controversy surrounding Nvidia's Jensen Huang or the Democratic sweep of Congress and its potential impact on data center expansion. But Brookings Institution senior fellow Robin Brooks blames the Federal Reserve. In a recent Substack post, Brooks argued that the Fed is worsening the market sell-off by signaling further rate hikes even as inflation expectations decline. Fed Governor Chris Waller, for example, said a 50-basis-point rate hike may be warranted in December to bring inflation back toward the Fed's 2% target. Meanwhile, data from Haver Analytics show that Brent crude prices and two-year inflation expectations have fallen, yet markets continue to expect higher interest rates. The result is a rise in real interest rates (nominal interest rates minus expected inflation). In effect, borrowing has become more expensive in inflation-adjusted terms, even without another Fed rate hike. "There's no doubt in my mind that the Fed is causing this meltdown," Brooks wrote. Even Wall Street's interest rate forecasts suggest the Fed may have to reverse course within a year. For example, Citigroup argues that financial markets are already signaling that interest rates are "unusually high" and will eventually need to come down. Citi expects just one more quarter-point rate hike in December, followed by a pause in early 2027 and cuts beginning in the second half of the year. It's an unusual forecast for a central bank that's supposedly still fighting inflation. The last time the Fed fought rising prices, it raised interest rates 11 times between March 2022 and July 2023, for a total increase of 5.25 percentage points. 📌 Bottom line: If Brooks is right, the Fed is making monetary policy more restrictive even before its next rate hike. And if Citi's forecast holds, investors may have to wait until the second half of 2027 for rate cuts.

title: US PCE Inflation Climbs to 3.8% as Core Rate Hits 3.3% - Limapagi
body: Persistent price pressures in the United States intensified in October 2026, with the latest government figures showing annual inflation rising to 3.8%. The Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) reported that core inflation also accelerated, complicating the economic outlook ahead of the Federal Reserve 's December interest rate decision. The Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index increased 0.3% from September, matching economists' expectations. On an annual basis, overall inflation advanced from 3.7% to 3.8%, according to the BEA's October report released on November 25. Core PCE, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, climbed to 3.3% from 3.1% in September. The increase exceeded the 3.2% forecast in a Bloomberg survey of economists published by U.S. Bank on November 20. Monthly core inflation nevertheless remained at 0.3%, matching both September's increase and economists' expectations. The annual core reading reached its highest level since November 2023, when inflation stood at 3.4%. The historical figures show that core inflation had generally remained between approximately 2.6% and 3.2% from the beginning of 2024 through September 2026. Overall inflation reached 3.8%, matching its May 2026 level and marking its highest reading since May 2023. Energy costs contributed to the divergence between overall and core inflation. The BEA's energy price index increased approximately 11.5% between February and March 2026 and stood 22.5% above its year-earlier level in October. Federal Reserve staff identified energy costs as an important factor behind the September inflation reading. Minutes from the central bank's October meeting described the movement as a “rapid increase in consumer energy prices,” while the BEA subsequently revised September's annual overall inflation figure from 3.6% to 3.7%. The Federal Reserve's October meeting minutes also indicated that almost all participating officials considered another increase in interest rates a possibility. The minutes stated that a further move “would likely be appropriate,” highlighting continuing concerns about inflationary pressures. The central bank's policy guidance explains that interest rate adjustments are “rapidly reflected” in the borrowing costs lenders charge on short-term loans. The October inflation report is therefore an important economic indicator ahead of the Federal Reserve's scheduled December 9 rate decision. The October core inflation figure also aligned with an estimate previously given by Federal Reserve official Michelle Bowman on November 10. However, it exceeded the estimate presented by Fed Governor Lisa Cook on November 20.
